analysis.one_liner: Extends pension, health, and unemployment protections to part-time and temporary workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it died with no cosponsors and no vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let workers who only want part-time hours collect unemployment benefits without being forced into full-time work, counted part-timers' hours toward pension participation and vesting, and required health plans to give part-time employees a proportionate share of the employer premium. It also would have treated long-term leased and contracted workers as employees for benefit plans, and taken aim at companies that wrongly label workers as independent contractors — barring willful misclassifiers from federal contracts and requiring bidders to certify their bids cover employment taxes. It also gave employers a waiver of back employment taxes for good-faith misclassification.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time and temporary workers — people putting in 500 to 1,000 hours a year who under ERISA rules could be kept out of pension plans entirely, and part-timers charged more for employer health coverage. Also workers falsely labeled independent contractors, who lose overtime, minimum wage, OSHA, and anti-discrimination protections, and honest government contractors bidding against misclassifiers who underbid by skipping payroll taxes.

how_it_helps.text: Amends federal unemployment rules so a person seeking part-time work cannot be denied benefits or forced to accept full-time work they didn't previously do [S2][S3].
Counts 500 hours of annual service as 1,000 for ERISA pension participation, vesting, and accrual rules, pulling part-timers into pension plans they are currently excluded from [S2][S3].

Bars group health plans from charging a part-time employee more than a ratable share of the full-time premium, and expands the ERISA definition of employee to cover workers leased or contracted to the same employer for a year or more at 500+ hours a year [S2][S3].

Bars companies finally determined to have willfully misclassified workers from federal procurement and defense contracts for two years, requires bidders to certify their bids cover employment taxes, and lets losing bidders sue over false certifications [S2][S3].

Tightens the 'safe harbor' that shields employers from payroll-tax liability for misclassifying workers, requiring an actual reasonable basis and repealing the rule that a prior audit blessing suffices [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who rely on part-time, temporary, leased, or misclassified workers — they would bear pension and health coverage costs for part-timers, payroll taxes for reclassified workers, and possible debarment from federal contracts. The tax-waiver provision would also forfeit some payroll-tax collections the government would otherwise recover from past misclassification.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using part-time and contract labor

drawbacks.text: The bill grants employers a full waiver of employment taxes, interest, and penalties for misclassified workers if they claim a good-faith misapplication of common-law tests — a concession that could reward misclassification rather than deter it [S2][S3].

Requiring health-plan premiums for part-timers and pension coverage at 500 hours raises benefit costs; an honest concern is that employers would respond by trimming hours below the thresholds or shifting more work to contractors outside the bill's reach [S3].
The bid-certification, notification, and debarment rules add compliance paperwork for contractors and subcontractors, including small firms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker protections are real but targeted: they cover people routinely written out of benefits by hour thresholds, and the contract-debarment provisions give the rules teeth. The bill is weakened by its own Title II tax waiver, which hands a generous escape hatch to employers caught misclassifying workers. On balance it is a modest, worker-favoring bill whose costs fall mainly on employers using contingent labor arrangements, with legitimate worry about hours-shrinking side effects.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors, sent to four committees, referred to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: Rep. Patricia Schroeder introduced the bill on June 19, 1996, with zero cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].

The Speaker referred it to four committees — Ways and Means, Economic and Educational Opportunities, Government Reform and Oversight, and National Security — splitting it across jurisdictions that each controlled a piece of it [S3][S5].

It was referred to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology on June 27 and the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations on July 8, with executive comment requested from the Department of Defense, and no further action followed [S5].
No floor vote ever occurred; the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on part-time, temporary, leased, and misclassified workers — and federal and defense contractors — kept the existing rules and avoided new coverage costs, certifications, and possible debarment.

for.name: Rep. Patricia Schroeder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: Presided over a House in which the bill never reached the floor for a vote

against.name: House Education and Workforce / Ways and Means subcommittees
against.role: Subcommittees on Employer-Employee Relations and Government Management, Information and Technology
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes or committee roll calls; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors in a Republican-controlled House, so partisan positions were never tested.

industries.industry: Temporary staffing and employee leasing firms
industries.note: The bill expands the ERISA definition of employee to cover long-term leased workers and requires pension and health-plan treatment of part-time and temporary staff — directly raising the cost of the staffing model these firms sell. Workers gain benefit access that the model currently avoids.

Willful misclassifiers would be barred from contracts for two years, bidders would have to certify their bids cover employment taxes, and rivals could sue over false certifications — adding compliance costs and real debarment risk.

The bill tightens the misclassification safe harbor and requires an actual reasonable basis, but it also waives back employment taxes, interest, and penalties for a good-faith misclassification — one hand tightens, the other forgives.

industries.industry: Retirement plan and benefits administration industry
industries.note: Extending plan coverage and prorating health premiums to part-timers would create new plan-participation, tracking, and compliance work for benefits administrators.
